questions.stem: The ACL below is applied inbound on a router interface. A packet from 10.1.4.20 to 10.1.9.80 on TCP port 22 arrives. What happens to it?
questions.exhibit:
access-list 120 permit tcp any host 10.1.9.80 eq 443
access-list 120 deny   tcp any host 10.1.9.80
access-list 120 permit ip 10.1.4.0 0.0.0.255 any

options.text: Denied by the second entry, before the third is checked
options.rationale: Correct: first match wins, and entry 2 matches.

options.text: Permitted by the third entry, which matches the source
options.rationale: Entry 3 would match, but entry 2 matches first.

options.text: Denied by the implicit deny at the end of the list
options.rationale: Denied, but by entry 2; the implicit deny is never reached.

options.text: Permitted, since permits outrank denies
options.rationale: Order decides, not the action.

questions.explanation: ACLs are ordered permit/deny statements processed top-down; the first match wins, and an implicit deny follows the last entry. The packet matches entry 2, so entry 3 is never checked.
questions.discriminator_tested: Top-down, first match wins; implicit deny at the end.

questions.stem: A standard ACL must stop subnet 10.1.4.0/24 from reaching the payroll server 10.1.9.5 while those users keep reaching everything else. Where should it be applied?

options.text: Near the payroll server
options.rationale: Correct: near the destination, it affects only traffic headed there.

options.text: Inbound on the users' router interface
options.rationale: Source-only filtering there would block the users from everything.

options.text: On each router between the two networks
options.rationale: Adds work and still blocks the users broadly wherever it sits near them.

options.text: At the internet edge router
options.rationale: Internal traffic never passes the internet edge.

questions.explanation: Standard ACLs filter on source IP only (numbered 1-99 and 1300-1999). Because they can't consider the destination, they are placed close to the destination; near the source they would block those users from everything.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard ACL: source only, so place close to the destination.

questions.stem: Which wildcard mask matches each host in 172.16.8.0/22?

options.rationale: Correct: the inverse of 255.255.252.0.
That is the subnet mask, not the wildcard.
That matches only a /24.
Not an inverse of any contiguous mask; it doesn't cover the /22.

questions.explanation: A wildcard mask is the inverse of a subnet mask: 0 means the bit must match and 1 means it is ignored. A /22 mask is 255.255.252.0, so the wildcard is 0.0.3.255.
questions.discriminator_tested: Wildcard = inverse mask; 0 must match, 1 ignored.

questions.stem: Users on 10.1.4.0/24 must be blocked from the HR server 10.1.9.20 on HTTPS, while all their other traffic flows. Which ACL type and placement BEST fit?

options.text: Extended ACL, close to the users' subnet
options.rationale: Correct: precise enough to place near the source.

options.text: Extended ACL, close to the HR server
options.rationale: Works, but the unwanted traffic crosses the network before being dropped.

options.text: Standard ACL, close to the HR server
options.rationale: A standard ACL can't single out HTTPS.

options.text: Standard ACL, close to the users' subnet
options.rationale: Source-only filtering there would cut the users off entirely.

questions.explanation: Extended ACLs filter on source, destination, protocol, and ports (100-199, 2000-2699). Because they are precise, they are placed close to the source, dropping unwanted traffic before it crosses the network.
questions.discriminator_tested: Extended ACL: granular, so place close to the source.

questions.stem: A router ACL permits outbound web traffic, but the replies are dropped unless a separate inbound rule allows them. Which device would admit the replies automatically?

options.text: A stateful firewall
options.rationale: Correct: it tracks sessions and admits their return traffic.

options.text: A standard ACL
options.rationale: ACLs are stateless; replies need their own rule.

options.text: An extended ACL
options.rationale: More granular, but still stateless.

options.text: A GRE tunnel
options.rationale: GRE encapsulates traffic; it doesn't filter or track it.

questions.explanation: Firewalls enforce policy between networks and add session awareness beyond ACL filtering. ACLs are stateless filters; a stateful firewall tracks sessions and admits their return traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: ACLs are stateless; stateful firewalls track sessions.

questions.stem: A file is encrypted with AES before being emailed. Which protection does that encryption provide by itself?

options.text: Keeping it confidential
options.rationale: Correct: only key holders can read it.

options.text: Proof of who sent the file
options.rationale: That needs authentication, such as a signature.

options.text: Detection of any change to the file
options.rationale: Integrity needs a hash or MAC; encryption alone doesn't provide it.

options.text: Compression to reduce the file's size
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't compress.

questions.explanation: Encryption converts plaintext to ciphertext with an algorithm and a key. It provides confidentiality; on its own it doesn't provide integrity or authentication.
questions.discriminator_tested: Encryption provides confidentiality, not integrity or authentication on its own.

questions.stem: Two offices want to encrypt a large nightly backup using the same secret key at both ends. What is the MAIN challenge of this approach?

options.text: Getting the shared key to both sites securely
options.rationale: Correct: key distribution is the symmetric challenge.

options.text: Keeping the key secret once both sites have it
options.rationale: Also needed, but distribution is the defining challenge.

options.text: The key must be published in a certificate
options.rationale: Certificates carry public keys; a shared secret key is never published.

options.text: Symmetric encryption is too slow for bulk data
options.rationale: Symmetric ciphers are the fast choice for bulk data.

questions.explanation: Symmetric key encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and suited to bulk data; key distribution is the challenge.
questions.discriminator_tested: Symmetric: fast, but key distribution is the challenge.

questions.stem: A legacy device can encrypt with DES and nothing else. What is the BEST assessment?

options.text: Its 56-bit key is breakable; replace the device
options.rationale: Correct: DES keys can be brute-forced.

options.text: Run DES three times for the same strength as AES
options.rationale: 3DES is itself deprecated and slower than AES.

options.text: DES is old, so performance will be poor
options.rationale: Speed isn't the problem; security is.

options.text: It is acceptable on an internal network
options.rationale: A breakable cipher is no protection inside either.

questions.explanation: DES uses a 56-bit key and 64-bit blocks. It is obsolete and insecure: the key can be brute-forced quickly.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why 3DES is no longer recommended, even though it isn't broken the way DES is?

options.text: It's a slow stopgap, replaced by AES
options.rationale: Correct: deprecated in favour of AES.

options.text: It applies DES three times
options.rationale: True, but that describes it rather than explaining why it is retired.

options.text: It uses a 56-bit key like DES
options.rationale: Its effective key is longer than DES's.

options.text: It is a hash function, not a cipher
options.rationale: 3DES is a block cipher.

questions.explanation: 3DES applies DES three times. It is a deprecated stopgap: slow, and replaced by AES.
questions.discriminator_tested: 3DES is a deprecated, slow stopgap replaced by AES.

questions.stem: Which algorithm should a new VPN use for bulk encryption of its traffic?

options.text: AES-256
options.rationale: Correct: the current standard symmetric cipher.

options.text: 3DES
options.rationale: Deprecated and slow.

options.text: DES
options.rationale: Obsolete and insecure.

options.text: MD5
options.rationale: A hash, not a cipher.

questions.explanation: AES, with 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys, is the current standard symmetric cipher. DES and 3DES are obsolete or deprecated, and MD5 is a hash, not a cipher.
questions.discriminator_tested: AES is the current standard symmetric cipher.

questions.stem: An engineer downloads a switch image and runs the command below. What does the match BEST confirm?
questions.exhibit:
Vendor page:  switch-ios.bin   SHA-256: 9F2C4E...7D0A71B

PS> Get-FileHash .\switch-ios.bin -Algorithm SHA256
Algorithm   Hash
SHA256      9F2C4E...7D0A71B

options.text: It is exactly the vendor's file
options.rationale: Correct: matching digests verify integrity.

options.text: It was transferred without errors
options.rationale: True, but it proves more: the file is exactly what the vendor published.

options.text: It is encrypted and safe to email
options.rationale: Hashing doesn't encrypt anything.

options.text: It can be reversed to recover the vendor's key
options.rationale: Hashes are one-way.

questions.explanation: A hash is a one-way function producing a fixed-length digest. Matching digests verify integrity; because a hash isn't reversible, it isn't encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hashes verify integrity; not reversible, so not encryption.

questions.stem: A software team still publishes MD5 checksums so customers can verify releases. What BEST describes the problem?

options.text: Its collisions can be forged
options.rationale: Correct: an attacker can craft a malicious file with the same digest.

options.text: MD5 produces a short 128-bit digest
options.rationale: True, but the real problem is that collisions are practical.

options.text: MD5 encrypts files, revealing their contents
options.rationale: MD5 is a hash; it doesn't encrypt.

options.text: MD5 is too slow for large release files
options.rationale: MD5 is fast; speed isn't the issue.

questions.explanation: MD5 produces a 128-bit digest and is broken: collisions can be produced, so it should be avoided for security use. SHA-256 or longer is preferred.
questions.discriminator_tested: MD5 is broken (collisions); avoid for security use.

questions.stem: A team is choosing a hash algorithm for verifying firmware images. Which choice is BEST?

options.text: SHA-256
options.rationale: Correct: a SHA-2 hash, preferred today.

options.text: SHA-1
options.rationale: Deprecated.

options.text: MD5
options.rationale: Broken by collisions.

options.text: AES-256
options.rationale: A cipher, not a hash.

questions.explanation: The Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) family includes SHA-1, SHA-2, and SHA-3. SHA-1 is deprecated; SHA-256 or longer is preferred.
questions.discriminator_tested: SHA-1 deprecated; SHA-256 or longer preferred.

questions.stem: Which two are typical VPN use cases? (Choose two.)

options.text: Staff working from home reaching internal apps
options.rationale: Correct: remote access (user to site).

options.text: Linking a branch office to headquarters over the internet
options.rationale: Correct: site-to-site.

options.text: Making public websites load faster for remote staff
options.rationale: A VPN adds overhead; it isn't a speed-up.

options.text: Replacing antivirus on remote laptops
options.rationale: A tunnel doesn't scan for malware.

options.text: Giving guests internet access on Wi-Fi
options.rationale: That is guest network isolation.

questions.explanation: A VPN is an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet. The two main uses are remote access (user to site) and site-to-site, and it is cheaper than leased lines.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes an enterprise VPN from a provider-managed VPN?

options.text: The organization runs it and owns its security
options.rationale: Correct: customer-controlled security.

options.text: It usually runs over the public internet
options.rationale: Often true, but control is the distinguishing point.

options.text: The provider isolates the customer's traffic
options.rationale: That describes a provider-managed VPN.

options.text: It doesn't use encryption
options.rationale: Enterprise VPNs such as IPsec and SSL VPNs encrypt.

questions.explanation: Enterprise VPNs are built and managed by the organization (IPsec, SSL VPN) over the internet, so the customer controls the security. A provider-managed VPN is operated by the service provider.

questions.stem: A company's sites connect over its carrier's MPLS VPN service. A regulator requires the traffic between sites to be encrypted. What is the BEST assessment?

options.text: It isolates; it doesn't encrypt
options.rationale: Correct: the provider separates traffic but doesn't necessarily encrypt it.

options.text: Traffic is isolated from other customers
options.rationale: True, but isolation doesn't meet an encryption requirement.

options.text: The provider is responsible for compliance
options.rationale: The company still owns its regulatory obligations.

options.text: MPLS VPNs include IPsec encryption
options.rationale: MPLS separates traffic with labels; it doesn't encrypt.

questions.explanation: Provider-managed VPNs, such as MPLS-based services, are operated by the service provider, which isolates customer traffic. That traffic is not necessarily encrypted, so encryption must be added if required.
questions.discriminator_tested: Provider-managed VPNs isolate but aren't necessarily encrypted.

questions.stem: Which two services does IPsec provide? (Choose two.)

options.text: Anti-replay protection
options.rationale: Correct: replayed packets are rejected.

options.text: Data origin authentication
options.rationale: Correct: packets are proven to come from the peer.

options.text: Malware scanning of tunneled traffic
options.rationale: IPsec protects traffic; it doesn't inspect content.

options.text: Name resolution for remote sites
options.rationale: That is DNS.

options.text: Application-layer content filtering
options.rationale: That is a proxy's or NGFW's job.

questions.explanation: IPsec is a suite securing IP traffic with confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and anti-replay. It is a framework (IKE plus AH/ESP), not a single protocol.
questions.discriminator_tested: IPsec is a framework: IKE plus AH/ESP.

questions.stem: A new site-to-site tunnel shows the output below. What does it BEST indicate?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show crypto isakmp sa
dst            src            state     status
203.0.113.2    198.51.100.1   QM_IDLE   ACTIVE

R1# show crypto ipsec sa | include pkts
    #pkts encaps: 0, #pkts encrypt: 0, #pkts digest: 0
    #pkts decaps: 0, #pkts decrypt: 0, #pkts verify: 0

options.text: Phase 1 up; no data through phase 2
options.rationale: Correct: QM_IDLE shows the IKE channel is up; zero counters show no data has used the tunnel.

options.text: The IKE management channel is established
options.rationale: True, but it ignores the zero data counters.

options.text: Phase 1 failed, so no data SAs were built
options.rationale: QM_IDLE and ACTIVE mean phase 1 succeeded.

options.text: Traffic is flowing but not being encrypted
options.rationale: No packets have been encapsulated at all.

questions.explanation: Cisco IOS IPsec is configured with an IKE policy, a transform set, and a crypto map or profile applied to an interface. IKE phase 1 builds the secure management channel (QM_IDLE means it is up); phase 2 builds the data SAs that carry traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: Phase 1 = management channel; phase 2 = data SAs.

questions.stem: Traffic between two sites must be encrypted as well as authenticated. Which IPsec protocol is required?

options.text: ESP (IP protocol 50)
options.rationale: Correct: ESP encrypts and also authenticates.

options.text: AH (IP protocol 51)
options.rationale: AH authenticates but doesn't encrypt.

options.text: GRE (IP protocol 47)
options.rationale: GRE encapsulates without encrypting.

options.text: IKE (UDP 500)
options.rationale: IKE negotiates keys; it doesn't carry the data.

questions.explanation: AH (protocol 51) provides integrity and authentication; ESP (protocol 50) provides encryption plus integrity and authentication. AH does not encrypt; ESP is the one that does.
questions.discriminator_tested: AH does not encrypt; ESP does.
